cells.tense: You are at the table, and you know what you are holding in your hands.
cells.ask: Pick one thing the group keeps returning to and give it a shape someone new could pick up. Before the week turns.
cells.core:
You are the one pressing what a group knows into a form that can outlast the evening. Not the loudest person at the table and not outside it — you take what is worth keeping and make it carryable, so it travels without you holding it up. The persistence is quiet and it is real: you stay with a thing long after attention has moved on, which is why what you touch tends to stay put.

There is a way this stays alive without turning into a monument. Practice can flow instead of being forced — the point is to keep the making honest, not to guard it. Time alone here connects rather than isolates, and the refining serves the work, not your worry about it. So put one piece of what this table knows into a form somebody else can lift.
cells.sheetLine: You build what a group keeps, and you keep it standing.
cells.verb: building something meant to last, pressing it into shape until it holds
cells.place: the shared table where a room's knowledge gets handed forward

cells.tense: You are already living in the version where it lands, and you are forcing it into being before it is ready.
cells.ask: Say it once, plainly, and let the room sit with it unanswered. No second pass tonight, no follow-up.
cells.core:
You are pushing what you want a group to carry harder than the group has asked for. Ahead of you there is a version where they finally get it the way you get it — and you are working backwards from there, so one talk at the table turns into an attempt to bring the room around. The building has turned into selling. The persistence that makes you good at this is now spending itself on a room that has not caught up yet.

What gets lost is the point the building was for: people pick a thing up because it moved them, not because they were handed it. The pressure reads as urgency, and the room feels managed rather than invited. Try saying it once and letting it stand there. What stays alive on its own was yours to begin with.

cells.tense: You stopped bringing it forward a while back, and you are still standing at a door you already walked through.
cells.ask: Walk into one room where this thing is already alive and be one person in it. Stay for the whole of it.
cells.core:
You know something a group needs and you are not putting it in front of them. The knowledge is still with you; the handing over stopped. You may tell yourself the timing is off or the room is not ready, but the door closed on your side, not theirs. Meanwhile the thing you care about is being kept by other people, in their words, in their hands.

What is missing is not the material. It is the willingness to stand in the middle of a room and take up your place there. That does not come from feeling your way back in; it comes from moving first. Go stand where the thing you care about is being kept by other people. Being one more person in the room is enough to start with.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what this group believes, and you talk about it as if it were happening on its own.
cells.ask: Name one thing you set in motion that the group now treats as just how it is. Say it out loud to one person.
cells.core:
Something in the way this group talks, the things they repeat, the habits they keep, came from you. You shaped it — in what you said and what you let stand — and you describe the result as if it had simply formed. The shaping keeps going. You just have not said it is yours. It is easier to call it the group's way than to say you made it.

The reason this matters is that what you built needs tending, and you cannot tend what you will not admit is yours. What you started had a feeling under it once, a real reason you cared. That is the thread back. Name the thing you set going and say it plainly to someone, and you get to keep it alive instead of watching it drift.
